source.title: What Cohort INRs Encode and Where to Freeze Them
source.authors: Vasiliki Sideri-Lampretsa; Sophie Starck; Robbie Holland; Julian McGinnis; Daniel Rueckert

page_placements.theme: Causal dictionary-feature interventions outside text-only LLMs

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies sparse autoencoders to INR activations in a new setting and reports single-atom ablations. These test whether the resulting atoms have causal effects, but do not directly test toy-model superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper motivates its SAE method by superposition and says the dictionary is overcomplete to accommodate it, but it does not measure feature overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transitions, or feature importance. Freeze-depth transfer results do not test the listed claim versions. The reported atom ablations and spatial firing patterns bear on whether SAE atoms function as representation units; they do not establish that the dictionaries are complete, stable, or canonical.
record.test_reason: The study uses TopK SAEs as an off-the-shelf probe of INR activations. It assumes superposition to justify an overcomplete dictionary (n=4096, 16× width) and reports only what its own atoms look like and do. It never measures feature overlap, near-orthogonality, sparsity transitions, capacity competition or polysemantic neurons (V1–V3). The models are INRs, not LLMs (V4). Showing that the top-magnitude atoms have causal effects does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable or canonical units (V5). Nothing bears on 1-D versus multi-dimensional features (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, but it omits the first main finding. The optimal test-time freeze depth coincides with the layer of peak weight stable rank (τ*=1 for SIREN, τ*=0 for FFMLP). Freezing there matches or beats STRAINER, with large Kodak gains. The authors also conclude that FFMLP deep atoms reflect memorized cohort content while SIREN atoms are content-independent positional tiles.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses TopK sparse autoencoders on INR activations and ablates individual dictionary atoms; it does not reproduce the toy-model experiments or measurements of Toy Models of Superposition.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported atom patterns and ablation effects vary by architecture and layer. The paper also reports an architectural split between cohort and single-signal INRs; SAE dictionary size n and TopK sparsity k are swept in supplementary diagnostics, but no stability or canonicality test is reported.

fits_no_version.finding: In cohort-trained SIREN and FFMLP INRs, ablating single top-magnitude SAE atoms reduces reconstruction PSNR. SIREN effects stay localized (0.2–9.2 dB). FFMLP effects are image-wide (up to 10.58 dB).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE atoms fitted to INR activations are causally used by the network, and their spatial character depends on architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Atom properties depend on SAE choices. In the (n,k) sweep, spatial L0 decreases strictly with dictionary size n at every (layer, k) cell. Dead-atom rates reach 59–74% in deep FFMLP layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In INRs, the SAE dictionary's atom geometry (locality) depends on dictionary size, so the decomposition is not unique.

record.code_released: not stated; the authors say they plan to release code upon acceptance.
record.problems: The evidence for atom effects includes selected ablations and reported maxima; uncertainty is not given for those ablation effects. The study tests only SIREN and FFMLP, and does not test completeness, run-to-run stability, or canonicality of the SAE decomposition.
record.rows_left_out: Freeze-depth transfer results, SAE hyperparameter sweeps, and atom firing/dead-atom statistics are not included because they do not directly test whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical representation units or the other listed claim versions.

untested.parts: Feature overlap and near-orthogonality, sparsity-dependent transition, geometry, interference. Superposition in INRs is assumed, not measured.
Capacity competition and dedicated versus shared dimensions. The paper informally speaks of 'spare capacity' filled with memorized content but measures nothing of the kind.
Polysemantic neurons and their causes are not studied.
No LLMs are studied. Whether the SAE recovers sparse features that the INR actually uses is not validated against ground truth.
No run-to-run stability, completeness or canonicality tests. Only causal ablation of top-magnitude atoms, plus a hyperparameter sweep used for selection.

record.verdict_notes: The reader marked V5 as tested and 'supports'. Causal relevance of a few selected top-magnitude atoms does not bear on whether dictionary features are complete, stable or canonical, so I reclassified the study as a tool use (T4) with no verdicts. The appendix (n,k) sweep shows atom locality changing monotonically with n. This could inform a V5 canonicality discussion, but it is a hyperparameter-selection diagnostic with no stability test. The authors say trends are stable around the chosen configuration, but they used only one SAE configuration and report no seeds. Preprint; code not released.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test toy-model superposition, feature-count pressure, overlap or near-orthogonality, interference, or dependence on sparsity and importance.
It does not test whether feature competition for capacity explains polysemantic neurons or dedicated dimensions.
It does not study polysemantic neurons or alternative causes of polysemanticity.
The models are INRs, not LLMs; it does not measure LLM features spread across neurons or SAE recovery in LLMs.
It tests causal effects of individual SAE atoms in INRs, but not whether the SAE dictionary is complete, stable across choices or runs, or a canonical decomposition.
SAE atoms are represented as individual decoder directions, but the study does not test whether the network’s underlying features are intrinsically one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: cohort-trained SIREN
rows.size_stated: 5 hidden layers, width d = 256; SAE dictionary n = 4096 atoms
rows.operation_detail: At layer ℓ2, remove a single SAE atom by subtracting its contribution from the activation.

conditions.value: CelebA cohort; ablation on a CelebA test image

rows.measure: PSNR drop and spatial distribution of reconstruction error
rows.baseline: Pre-ablation reconstruction; exact PSNR not stated
rows.value: PSNR drops by 2-3 dB, concentrated in the region where the atom fires; error is spatially localized.
rows.note: The paper reports that the ablation effect stays confined to the atom’s firing region. This supports causal use of these atoms, not dictionary completeness or canonicality.
rows.check: Single-atom ablation PSNR drops show that selected SAE atoms causally affect output. They do not measure completeness, stability or canonicality of the dictionary, so no version is tested. The ablated atoms were chosen as the top-2 by mean magnitude at ℓ2.

relation.reason: Superposition motivates the overcomplete dictionary in Secs. 3.3 and 4.2; the reported interventions establish causal reconstruction effects of selected atoms without testing a listed claim version.

tranche.reason: Uses overcomplete TopK SAEs to investigate INR representations and reconstruction effects. It does not test toy-model superposition, capacity-driven polysemanticity, LLM representations, dictionary completeness or canonicality, or feature dimensionality.

source_check.notes: Main-text ablations select the top-2 atoms at ℓ2; Appendix C selects the top-4 per layer. Exact pre-ablation PSNR values are unavailable in the supplied text, although captions describe figure annotations.
